content: Lesson 45 guessed about NOW with must,
might and can't. To guess about the
PAST, add have + the past participle.
SURE it happened — must have done:
"The siren must have scared him off."
MAYBE — might/could have done:
"She might have taken the wrong bag."
"It could have been an accident."
SURE it did NOT happen — can't have done:
"He can't have taken the wallet; he was
with me all evening."
As before, the 'no' of must have is
can't have, never mustn't have.
Use these to accuse or to defend on the
evidence: "You can't have seen him — he
had already left."
Many languages weigh a past guess with
an adverb like 'probably'; English bends
must, might and can't onto have + done.
These words all set up a contrast — an
'even so'. They differ in what follows.
although / though + a full clause
(subject + verb):
"Although the industry was small, its
influence was huge."
despite / in spite of + a noun or -ing
(no clause):
"Despite its size, the industry led."
"In spite of losing, they smiled."
however joins two SENTENCES. It stands
apart, usually after a full stop or
semicolon, with a comma:
"The plan was bold. However, it failed."
"It was late; however, we went on."
So: although inside one sentence,
however between two, despite before a
noun. Same contrast, three tools.
Many languages carry contrast on one
small word that fits anywhere; English
sorts it by what follows — a clause, a
noun, or a whole new sentence.
In reading you will meet clauses that
drop 'who/which is' and lead with a
participle. Read them like this:
-ing = active (who is doing it):
"The man standing at the gate waved."
= the man WHO IS standing.
-ed/-en = passive (done to it):
"A robot built in Japan arrived."
= a robot WHICH WAS built in Japan.
A participle clause can also open a
sentence, setting the scene:
"Having finished training, they rested."
"Built over five tiers, your English
stands."
And that last line is true. You opened
Core naming to be; you leave holding the
perfect, the passive, reported speech,
the conditionals and the words that join
whole thoughts. The exit is a door onto
real text — walk through it.
Many languages spell out every 'who was'
and 'after they had'; English lets a
lone participle carry the clause — and
now you can read it.
